title: Securing Controlled Stock, Reporting Theft or Loss, and Disposing of It Lawfully
subtopic: Physical and personnel security of the controlled stock, the theft-or-loss report, and the permitted disposal routes with their destruction standard and records
learning_objectives: State what 247 CMR 9.21 requires of a Massachusetts pharmacy: where controlled substances are stored, the three permitted arrangements for Schedules II through V, and what the alarm, camera and barrier paragraphs demand.
Say who is responsible for pharmacy security and access to the prescription area, and who may and may not make entries in or adjustments to the Schedule II perpetual inventory.
Apply 105 CMR 700.005(B): when the screening happens, the single purpose it serves, where the documentation goes, and why the employment bar in 105 CMR 700.005(B)(2) has no look-back period.
Separate a discrepancy found on a count from a reportable event, and name the two federal clocks that both start at discovery of a theft or significant loss.
List the factors 21 CFR 1301.74(c) tells a registrant to weigh in judging whether a loss is significant, and state what the paragraph says about substances that are later recovered.
Name the ways 21 CFR 1317.05(a) allows a practitioner to dispose of controlled substances in its own inventory, and identify the route that is written for non-practitioners only.
State the non-retrievable standard in 21 CFR 1317.90 and match each destination in 21 CFR 1317.95 to the two-employee procedure it carries.
Say when a DEA Form 41 is the required record of destruction under 21 CFR 1304.21(e), when it is not, and what separate use 21 CFR 1317.05(a)(4) makes of the same form.
State the reverse distributor's own registration duty, the delivery controls in 21 CFR 1317.15(b), and the 30-calendar-day destruction deadline in 21 CFR 1317.15(d).

orientation.text: Security in a Massachusetts pharmacy is a list of checkable conditions rather than a general aspiration, and 247 CMR 9.21 states them one at a time. All controlled substances are stored within the secured prescription area and in a safe and secure manner. Schedules II through V are stored in a securely locked and substantially constructed cabinet, or a similarly secured storage area, or dispersed throughout the stock of Schedule VI controlled substances in such a manner as to obstruct theft and diversion, so dispersal is a third permitted arrangement rather than a relaxation of the first two. The pharmacy maintains a centrally monitored security system that is able to detect a breach in security and is designed to prevent theft, and activates it when the pharmacy is closed. It maintains surveillance cameras in a manner designed to record theft and diversion of controlled substances, and retains video records for at least 14 days or, in the case of known or suspected theft or diversion, at least two years. A pharmacy located within another retail establishment is secured by a floor to ceiling barrier, securely locked and separately alarmed at all times when the pharmacy is closed. All drug order deliveries containing controlled substances are delivered directly to the pharmacy. None of this switches off for stock the pharmacy no longer wants, because 247 CMR 9.21(10) applies each requirement of the section to controlled substances that are expired, quarantined, or pending reverse distribution.

Who may be near the stock is settled in two places that answer different questions. 247 CMR 9.21(6) fixes responsibility inside the pharmacy: the pharmacist Manager of Record and the pharmacist on duty are responsible for pharmacy security and shall control access to the prescription area. The perpetual-inventory paragraph narrows that further, providing that an inventory adjustment resulting from a discrepancy is performed only by the pharmacist Manager of Record, or in the Manager of Record's absence by a pharmacist designee who then reports to the Manager of Record, that an unlicensed individual may not make any entry into or adjust the perpetual inventory, and that a certified pharmacy technician may make entries. 105 CMR 700.005(B) governs the earlier question of who is hired at all. All applicants and registrants shall screen before employment new employees who may work in or around areas where controlled substances are handled; under 105 CMR 700.005(B)(1) that screening is made solely for the purpose of determining whether the prospective employee is a responsible person who can be trusted to work in and around controlled substances, and documentation of the screening is made available to the Commissioner upon his or her request rather than filed in advance. 105 CMR 700.005(B)(2) then states a bar: no registrant shall knowingly employ any agent or employee who has had an application for registration denied for violation of any law or regulation, or has had his or her registration revoked for violation of any law or regulation, at any time. The closing words carry the weight, because they leave no look-back period against which clean years could run.

A missing quantity is not automatically a reportable event, and the sequence matters. 247 CMR 9.21(8)(c) requires a pharmacy to reconcile the perpetual inventory for each Schedule II controlled substance at least once every ten days by performing an accurate physical count of inventory on hand and comparing it with the perpetual inventory, and it then puts the next step on one person: the Manager of Record shall investigate any discrepancy and report any significant loss or suspected theft in accordance with federal and state requirements. The federal requirement appears at 21 CFR 1301.74(c). The registrant must notify the Field Division Office of the Administration in his or her area, in writing, of any theft or significant loss of any controlled substances within one business day of discovery of the theft or loss, and must also file a complete and accurate DEA Form 106 with the Administration through the DEA Diversion Control Division secure network application within 45 calendar days after discovery. Those are two duties running on two clocks, not one duty with a long deadline. The paragraph adds that thefts and significant losses must be reported whether or not the controlled substances are subsequently recovered or the responsible parties are identified and action taken against them, and it allocates in-transit losses: unless the theft or loss occurs during an import or export transaction, the supplier is responsible for reporting an in-transit loss by its agent or by the common or contract carrier it selected, within one business day of discovery. Significance is judged rather than counted, against the factors the paragraph supplies: the actual quantity lost in relation to the type of business, the specific substances lost, whether the loss can be associated with access by specific individuals or attributed to unique activities, a pattern of losses over a specific time period with the results of efforts taken to resolve them, and, if known, whether the substances are likely candidates for diversion together with local trends and other indicators of diversion potential.

Disposal is not ordinary waste handling with extra paperwork. It is a separate scheme with its own part of the regulations, its own permitted destinations and its own witnessing rules, so the answer cannot be reached by asking what is convenient or what the state's waste rules would tolerate. 21 CFR 1317.05(a) opens with a closed list: a registered practitioner in lawful possession of a controlled substance in its inventory that desires to dispose of that substance shall do so in one of the following ways. Those ways are prompt destruction in accordance with subpart C of part 1317 using an on-site method of destruction; prompt delivery to a reverse distributor's registered location, by common or contract carrier pick-up or by reverse distributor pick-up at the registrant's registered location; prompt delivery, for the purpose of return or recall, to the registered person from whom the substance was obtained, to the registered manufacturer of the substance, or to another registrant the manufacturer has authorized to accept returns or recalls on its behalf; and a request for assistance from the Special Agent in Charge of the Administration in the area in which the practitioner is located. A retail pharmacy is a practitioner for these purposes, as 21 CFR 1317.05 says in terms when it describes collectors that are practitioners as retail pharmacies and hospitals or clinics. The route that lets a registrant carry the substances to the destruction site by its own means is written into 21 CFR 1317.05(b) for non-practitioners, and so is not on the practitioner's list.

Whichever route is chosen, the destruction standard and the record are fixed. 21 CFR 1317.90 requires all controlled substances to be destroyed by a registrant, or caused to be destroyed by a registrant under 21 CFR 1317.95(c), to be destroyed in compliance with applicable Federal, State, tribal and local laws and regulations and to be rendered non-retrievable. Where multiple controlled substances are comingled the method must be sufficient to render all of them non-retrievable, and where the substances collected for destruction are unknown but may reasonably include controlled substances the method must be sufficient to render non-retrievable any controlled substance likely to be present. Non-retrievable is a defined term for the purposes of the disposal part: the substance's physical or chemical condition or state is permanently altered through irreversible means, so that it is unavailable and unusable for all practical purposes and cannot be transformed back into a controlled substance or a controlled substance analogue. 21 CFR 1317.95 then attaches two employees to every destination, and 21 CFR 1304.21(e) attaches the record to only two of them: any registered person that destroys a controlled substance under 21 CFR 1317.95(d), or causes the destruction of a controlled substance under 21 CFR 1317.95(c), shall maintain a record of destruction on a DEA Form 41 that is complete and accurate and includes the name and signature of the two employees who witnessed the destruction. Massachusetts layers its own record on top: 247 CMR 9.21(9) requires a pharmacy to maintain an accurate record of all controlled substances returned to a reverse distributor or disposed of in accordance with state and federal laws and regulations, including proper DEA forms in the case of Schedule II controlled substances.

worked_examples.scenario: A Massachusetts pharmacy runs its ten-day Schedule II reconciliation and finds 40 tablets of one product on hand against a perpetual-inventory balance of 70. A technician offers to correct the record to match the count so that the next reconciliation starts clean, and the pharmacist on duty suggests waiting until month end to see whether the numbers settle before telling anyone.
steps: Separate the count from the conclusion. 247 CMR 9.21(8)(c) requires the reconciliation at least once every ten days and then requires the Manager of Record to investigate any discrepancy, so the count triggers an investigation rather than itself establishing a loss.

Fix who may touch the record. 247 CMR 9.21(8) permits an inventory adjustment resulting from a discrepancy to be performed only by the pharmacist Manager of Record, or by a pharmacist designee in the Manager of Record's absence who then reports to the Manager of Record, and it bars an unlicensed individual from making any entry into or adjusting the perpetual inventory.

Judge significance against the factors 21 CFR 1301.74(c) supplies rather than against a threshold: the actual quantity in relation to the type of business, the specific substance, whether the loss can be associated with access by specific individuals or attributed to unique activities, any pattern over a specific time period with the results of efforts to resolve it, and, if known, the diversion potential of the substance and local trends.

If the investigation establishes a theft or significant loss, start both federal clocks from discovery: written notice to the Field Division Office of the Administration in the registrant's area within one business day, and a complete and accurate DEA Form 106 through the DEA Diversion Control Division secure network application within 45 calendar days.

Preserve the evidence the state rule expects to exist. 247 CMR 9.21(4) requires video records to be retained for at least two years where theft or diversion is known or suspected, rather than the ordinary 14 days.
worked_examples.resolution: The Manager of Record investigates, the technician does not adjust the record, and the one-business-day written notice runs from discovery if the investigation establishes a theft or significant loss. The error the scenario invites is treating an inventory adjustment as the response to a discrepancy, which destroys the evidence the investigation needs; the second error is letting a wait-and-see period run against a clock the regulation starts at discovery rather than at proof.

worked_examples.scenario: A pharmacy has expired Schedule II and Schedule IV stock sitting in a quarantine bin on an open shelf, waiting for the reverse distributor's next pick-up. A technician has already filled out a DEA Form 41 for the bin so the paperwork will be ready, and an intern asks whether the bin still has to sit inside the secured storage now that the drugs can no longer be dispensed.
steps: Name the route. Delivery to a reverse distributor's registered location, by common or contract carrier pick-up or by reverse distributor pick-up at the pharmacy's registered location, is one of the ways 21 CFR 1317.05(a) allows a practitioner to dispose of inventory.

Check the recipient's status rather than its business description. 21 CFR 1317.15(a) requires any person that reverse distributes a controlled substance to be registered with the Administration as a reverse distributor unless exempted by law or otherwise authorized.

Apply 21 CFR 1317.95 to the hand-over itself. A transfer to a person registered or authorized to accept the substances for destruction falls under paragraph (a), so two employees of the transferring registrant load and unload, or observe the loading and unloading, until the transfer is complete.

Ask what 21 CFR 1304.21(e) actually attaches the Form 41 to. It is the record for a registered person that destroys a controlled substance under 21 CFR 1317.95(d) or causes destruction under 21 CFR 1317.95(c); handing stock to a reverse distributor is neither, so the pharmacy destroys nothing and creates no such record.

Answer the intern from 247 CMR 9.21(10), which applies each requirement of the section to controlled substances that are expired, quarantined, or pending reverse distribution, so the bin belongs inside the security the section requires.

Note where the duty travels next. 21 CFR 1317.15(d) requires the reverse distributor to destroy or cause the destruction of any controlled substance received for the purpose of destruction no later than 30 calendar days after receipt.
worked_examples.resolution: The bin goes back into secured storage, the pick-up follows the two-employee transfer procedure, and the pharmacy records the transfer under 247 CMR 9.21(9) rather than on a Form 41. The error the scenario invites is treating the DEA Form 41 as a receipt for anything that leaves the pharmacy for disposal, when it is a record of destruction; the second error is assuming that stock which can no longer be dispensed has passed out of the reach of the security rule.

worked_examples.scenario: A Massachusetts pharmacy is hiring a stock assistant who will unpack deliveries in the prescription area beside the controlled-substance cabinet. Nine years ago the applicant's own registration was revoked for a regulatory violation, and he has worked without incident since. The manager proposes to hire him, record the history in the personnel file, keep him away from the cabinet itself, and file the screening paperwork with the Department so that the record is on file in advance.
steps: Ask first who has to be screened. 105 CMR 700.005(B) reaches new employees who may work in or around areas where controlled substances are handled, and unpacking deliveries in the prescription area is work in and around such an area.

Read the purpose clause before treating this as an ordinary background check. Under 105 CMR 700.005(B)(1) the screening is made solely for the purpose of determining whether the prospective employee is a responsible person who can be trusted to work in and around controlled substances.

Place the documentation correctly. The same paragraph requires documentation of the screening to be made available by applicants and registrants to the Commissioner upon his or her request, which is a duty to produce on request rather than a duty to file in advance.

Apply the bar in 105 CMR 700.005(B)(2). No registrant shall knowingly employ any agent or employee who has had an application for registration denied for violation of any law or regulation, or has had his or her registration revoked for violation of any law or regulation, at any time.

Test each proposed workaround against the words of the bar. It prohibits employing the person, so narrowing his duties does not answer it, and it ends with the words at any time, so nine clean years do not answer it either.

Remember that hiring is not the only access control. 247 CMR 9.21(6) makes the pharmacist Manager of Record and the pharmacist on duty responsible for pharmacy security and requires them to control access to the prescription area, so even a lawful hire does not arrive with unrestricted access.
worked_examples.resolution: The pharmacy may not knowingly employ him in this role. The error the scenario invites is importing a look-back period the regulation does not contain, and then reaching for mitigation devices, a documented history, restricted duties, or a filing with the Department, none of which 105 CMR 700.005(B)(2) offers as a route around a bar written without one.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Where does 247 CMR 9.21 require a pharmacy to store controlled substances, and what are the three permitted arrangements for Schedules II through V?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Within the secured prescription area and in a safe and secure manner. Schedules II through V go in a securely locked and substantially constructed cabinet, or a similarly secured storage area, or dispersed throughout the stock of Schedule VI controlled substances in such a manner as to obstruct theft and diversion.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: How long must a Massachusetts pharmacy retain surveillance video records, and what changes the answer?
retrieval_prompts.answer: At least 14 days, and at least two years in the case of known or suspected theft or diversion.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Who is responsible for pharmacy security under 247 CMR 9.21, and who may make entries in or adjustments to the Schedule II perpetual inventory?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The pharmacist Manager of Record and the pharmacist on duty are responsible and control access to the prescription area. A certified pharmacy technician may make entries; an unlicensed individual may not make any entry or adjustment; and an adjustment resulting from a discrepancy is performed only by the Manager of Record, or by a pharmacist designee in the Manager of Record's absence who then reports to the Manager of Record.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: When does the screening in 105 CMR 700.005(B) happen, what single purpose does it serve, and where does the documentation go?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Before employment, for new employees who may work in or around areas where controlled substances are handled; solely to determine whether the prospective employee is a responsible person who can be trusted to work in and around controlled substances; and the documentation is made available to the Commissioner upon his or her request.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: State the employment bar in 105 CMR 700.005(B)(2) and the words that decide how long it lasts.
retrieval_prompts.answer: No registrant shall knowingly employ any agent or employee who has had an application for registration denied for violation of any law or regulation, or has had his or her registration revoked for violation of any law or regulation, at any time. The closing words at any time leave no look-back period.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Two clocks start when a theft or significant loss is discovered. Name each and say what it requires.
retrieval_prompts.answer: Written notice to the Field Division Office of the Administration in the registrant's area within one business day of discovery, and a complete and accurate DEA Form 106 filed with the Administration through the DEA Diversion Control Division secure network application within 45 calendar days after discovery.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Does recovering the stock, or identifying who took it, remove the federal reporting duty?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. Thefts and significant losses must be reported whether or not the controlled substances are subsequently recovered or the responsible parties are identified and action taken against them.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Name the ways 21 CFR 1317.05(a) allows a practitioner to dispose of a controlled substance in its own inventory.
retrieval_prompts.answer: Prompt on-site destruction in accordance with subpart C of part 1317; prompt delivery to a reverse distributor's registered location; prompt delivery for return or recall to the registered person from whom it was obtained, the registered manufacturer, or another registrant the manufacturer authorized to accept returns or recalls; and a request for assistance from the Special Agent in Charge in the practitioner's area, made by submitting one copy of a DEA Form 41 listing the substances.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What does non-retrievable mean, and what does 21 CFR 1317.90 require where substances are comingled or unidentified?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The substance's physical or chemical condition or state is permanently altered through irreversible means so that it is unavailable and unusable for all practical purposes and cannot be transformed back into a controlled substance or analogue. Where substances are comingled the method must render all of them non-retrievable, and where the substances collected are unknown but may reasonably include controlled substances the method must be sufficient for any controlled substance likely to be present.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which two paragraphs of 21 CFR 1317.95 make a DEA Form 41 the required record, and what must that record contain?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Paragraph (d), on-site destruction, and paragraph (c), causing destruction after transport to a location that is not registered. Under 21 CFR 1304.21(e) the record must be complete and accurate and include the name and signature of the two employees who witnessed the destruction.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: How soon must a reverse distributor destroy a controlled substance it received for destruction, and where may a delivery to it be made?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No later than 30 calendar days after receipt. Delivery may be made only to the reverse distributor at its registered location, may not be re-routed to any other location or person once en route regardless of registration status, and must be personally received by an employee of the reverse distributor at the registered location.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which controlled stock does 247 CMR 9.21 stop protecting once it has been set aside for disposal?
retrieval_prompts.answer: None. 247 CMR 9.21(10) applies each requirement of the section to controlled substances that are expired, quarantined, or pending reverse distribution.

21 CFR 1317.05(a) states a closed list of the ways a practitioner may dispose of a controlled substance in its inventory: prompt on-site destruction, prompt delivery to a reverse distributor's registered location, prompt delivery for return or recall, or a request for assistance from the Special Agent in Charge.

decision_logic.condition: Controlled stock is being put away, locked up or left overnight in a Massachusetts pharmacy.
decision_logic.action: Apply 247 CMR 9.21 paragraph by paragraph: the secured prescription area, one of the three permitted arrangements for Schedules II through V, the centrally monitored system activated at closing, cameras with the retention the section sets, and, inside another retail establishment, the floor to ceiling barrier securely locked and separately alarmed.

decision_logic.condition: A new employee will work in or around an area where controlled substances are handled.
decision_logic.action: Screen before employment for trustworthiness around controlled substances, keep the documentation available for the Commissioner on request, and check 105 CMR 700.005(B)(2) before extending an offer, because a denied application or a revoked registration for violation of any law or regulation bars knowing employment at any time.

decision_logic.condition: A ten-day Schedule II reconciliation, or any other count, produces a discrepancy.
decision_logic.action: Have the Manager of Record investigate before anyone adjusts the record, and let only the Manager of Record, or a pharmacist designee in the Manager of Record's absence, make an adjustment arising from that discrepancy.

decision_logic.condition: The investigation establishes a theft or significant loss of controlled substances.
decision_logic.action: Send written notice to the Field Division Office of the Administration in the registrant's area within one business day of discovery, and file a complete and accurate DEA Form 106 through the DEA Diversion Control Division secure network application within 45 calendar days after discovery, whether or not the substances are later recovered.

decision_logic.condition: Stock is expired, quarantined or otherwise unwanted and has to leave the pharmacy's usable inventory.
decision_logic.action: Pick one of the routes 21 CFR 1317.05(a) lists for a practitioner and act promptly; do not invent a route, and do not treat transport by the pharmacy's own means to a destruction site as one of them.

decision_logic.condition: A vendor offers to collect unwanted controlled stock for disposal.
decision_logic.action: Confirm the vendor is registered with the Administration as a reverse distributor, deliver only to its registered location by an authorized pick-up or carrier, and expect it to destroy or cause the destruction of the substances no later than 30 calendar days after receipt.

decision_logic.condition: The pharmacy itself will destroy controlled substances rather than transfer them.
decision_logic.action: Render them non-retrievable in compliance with applicable Federal, State, tribal and local laws and regulations, and run the two-employee procedure 21 CFR 1317.95 attaches to the destination, including personal witnessing of the destruction under paragraphs (c) and (d).

decision_logic.condition: The destruction or the transfer is finished and someone asks which record to create.
decision_logic.action: Create a DEA Form 41 only where 21 CFR 1304.21(e) requires it, namely destruction under 21 CFR 1317.95(d) or causing destruction under 21 CFR 1317.95(c), and in either case record the name and signature of the two employees who witnessed the destruction.

decision_logic.condition: The stock being disposed of includes Schedule II product, and the pharmacy is in Massachusetts.
decision_logic.action: Keep the accurate record 247 CMR 9.21(9) requires of all controlled substances returned to a reverse distributor or disposed of, including the proper DEA forms for Schedule II, and keep the stock inside the section's security until it leaves.

ma_vs_federal.text: The Massachusetts storage rule is written for a pharmacy and is more specific than a general security duty: 247 CMR 9.21 names the secured prescription area, the three permitted arrangements for Schedules II through V, a centrally monitored system activated at closing, cameras with a defined retention period, and a floor to ceiling barrier for a pharmacy inside another retail establishment.

The federal theft-or-loss duty runs to the Administration, while Massachusetts routes the same event through the Manager of Record: 247 CMR 9.21(8)(c) requires that person to investigate any discrepancy and to report any significant loss or suspected theft in accordance with federal and state requirements, so the state rule points back at 21 CFR 1301.74(c) rather than replacing it.

Disposal records stack rather than substitute. The federal record of destruction is the DEA Form 41 required by 21 CFR 1304.21(e), while 247 CMR 9.21(9) separately requires an accurate record of all controlled substances returned to a reverse distributor or disposed of, including proper DEA forms in the case of Schedule II controlled substances.

Federal law decides where unwanted stock may go, and Massachusetts decides how it is held until it goes: 21 CFR 1317.05(a) fixes the practitioner's routes, while 247 CMR 9.21(10) applies every security requirement of the section to controlled substances that are expired, quarantined, or pending reverse distribution.

The Massachusetts personnel bar is a state-law hiring prohibition addressed to registrants under 105 CMR 700.005(B)(2), enforced through the Commissioner's power to demand the screening documentation on request rather than through any advance filing.

exceptions.text: 247 CMR 9.21(11) provides that the requirements of 247 CMR 9.21 do not apply to non-resident pharmacies.
247 CMR 9.21(12) sends an institutional sterile compounding pharmacy to a different source, requiring it to store and secure controlled substances in accordance with 105 CMR 700.000.

Dispersal is the alternative built into 247 CMR 9.21(2): Schedules II through V need not sit in a cabinet if they are dispersed throughout the stock of Schedule VI controlled substances in such a manner as to obstruct theft and diversion.
105 CMR 700.005(B)(2) is written without a look-back period, a cure or a waiver, so there is no exception to find; the words at any time are the operative limit.

21 CFR 1301.74(c) allocates in-transit losses away from the receiving registrant: unless the theft or loss occurs during an import or export transaction, the supplier is responsible for reporting an in-transit loss by its agent or by the common or contract carrier it selected, within one business day of discovery.

21 CFR 1304.21(e) carves out one destruction from the Form 41 requirement: a controlled substance dispensed by a practitioner for immediate administration at the practitioner's registered location that is not fully exhausted is recorded under the ordinary dispensing-record provision instead.

21 CFR 1317.05(a)(5) allows a standing arrangement where a practitioner is required regularly to dispose of controlled substances: the Special Agent in Charge may authorize disposal without a prior application in each instance, on the condition that the practitioner keeps records of the disposals and files periodic reports summarising them, and may attach further conditions.

timing_deadlines.event: Written notice of a theft or significant loss of controlled substances
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Within one business day of discovery of the theft or loss
timing_deadlines.consequence: Notice goes in writing to the Field Division Office of the Administration in the registrant's area, and the duty does not wait for the investigation to finish.

timing_deadlines.event: Filing the DEA Form 106 for that theft or loss
timing_deadlines.consequence: A complete and accurate Form 106 is filed with the Administration through the DEA Diversion Control Division secure network application; this is a second duty, not an extension of the first.

timing_deadlines.event: Reporting an in-transit loss outside an import or export transaction
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Within one business day of discovery
timing_deadlines.consequence: The supplier, not the receiving registrant, reports the loss by its agent or by the common or contract carrier it selected.

timing_deadlines.event: Reconciling the Schedule II perpetual inventory
timing_deadlines.timeframe: At least once every ten days
timing_deadlines.consequence: An accurate physical count of inventory on hand is compared with the perpetual inventory, and any discrepancy goes to the Manager of Record to investigate.
Ordinary retention for cameras maintained in a manner designed to record theft and diversion of controlled substances.

timing_deadlines.event: Retention of surveillance video where theft or diversion is known or suspected
timing_deadlines.consequence: The longer period attaches to the same recordings once theft or diversion is known or suspected, so a decision to delete on the ordinary schedule can destroy the evidence the state rule expects to survive.

timing_deadlines.event: Activation of the pharmacy's centrally monitored security system
timing_deadlines.consequence: A pharmacy inside another retail establishment must in addition be securely locked and separately alarmed at all times when the pharmacy is closed.

timing_deadlines.event: Screening a prospective employee who may work in or around areas where controlled substances are handled
timing_deadlines.consequence: The screening is a condition of hiring rather than an onboarding step, and its documentation must be available to the Commissioner upon request.

timing_deadlines.event: Duration of the bar on knowingly employing a person whose application was denied or whose registration was revoked for violation of any law or regulation
timing_deadlines.timeframe: At any time, with no look-back period
timing_deadlines.consequence: The passage of incident-free years does not lift the bar, and no documentation, restriction of duties or notification is offered as a substitute.

timing_deadlines.event: Destruction by a reverse distributor of substances received for the purpose of destruction
timing_deadlines.timeframe: No later than 30 calendar days after receipt
timing_deadlines.consequence: The reverse distributor destroys or causes the destruction of the substances within that period, having stored them under the security controls in parts 1301 and 1317 in the meantime.

timing_deadlines.event: Acting on a decision to dispose of controlled substances in a practitioner's inventory
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Promptly, in the terms 21 CFR 1317.05(a) uses for each route
timing_deadlines.consequence: Destruction, delivery to a reverse distributor and delivery for return or recall are each required to be prompt, so unwanted stock is not left to accumulate under the security rules indefinitely.

forms_records.text: DEA Form 106 is the theft-or-loss filing: complete and accurate, submitted to the Administration through the DEA Diversion Control Division secure network application within 45 calendar days after discovery, and preceded by written notice to the Field Division Office within one business day.
The one-business-day notice is itself a written record, addressed to the Field Division Office of the Administration in the registrant's area rather than to a state agency.

DEA Form 41 is the record of destruction required by 21 CFR 1304.21(e) from any registered person that destroys a controlled substance under 21 CFR 1317.95(d) or causes destruction under 21 CFR 1317.95(c); it must be complete and accurate and include the name and signature of the two employees who witnessed the destruction.

A DEA Form 41 is not the record for handing stock to a reverse distributor or for transporting it to a registered location, because 21 CFR 1304.21(e) attaches the record only to the two destruction paragraphs of 21 CFR 1317.95.

The same form has a second and different use: 21 CFR 1317.05(a)(4) has a practitioner submit one copy of a DEA Form 41 to the Special Agent in Charge, listing the controlled substances it desires to dispose of, in order to request disposal assistance.

Where the Special Agent in Charge authorises a practitioner that regularly disposes of controlled substances to act without a prior application in each instance, the practitioner keeps records of those disposals and files periodic reports summarising them.

247 CMR 9.21(9) requires a pharmacy to maintain an accurate record of all controlled substances returned to a reverse distributor or disposed of in accordance with state and federal laws and regulations, including proper DEA forms in the case of Schedule II controlled substances.

The Schedule II perpetual inventory is itself a security record: it may be kept in hard copy or electronically, must reflect the amount of each Schedule II controlled substance located on the pharmacy premises, and covers each such substance the pharmacy has received, dispensed, or disposed of.

That record must include the name and strength of each Schedule II controlled substance, the quantity of each drug purchased or added to inventory, the starting inventory, prescription numbers, the dispensed quantity, the remaining balance, and pharmacist identification for each transaction.
Surveillance video is a record with its own retention rule, kept at least 14 days and at least two years where theft or diversion is known or suspected.
Documentation of pre-employment screening is retained so that it can be made available by applicants and registrants to the Commissioner upon his or her request.

role_duties.duty: Is responsible for pharmacy security together with the pharmacist on duty, controls access to the prescription area, investigates any discrepancy found on the Schedule II reconciliation, reports any significant loss or suspected theft in accordance with federal and state requirements, and is the only person who may make an inventory adjustment resulting from a discrepancy.
May make an inventory adjustment resulting from a discrepancy in the Manager of Record's absence, and then reports the change to the Manager of Record.
May make entries into the Schedule II perpetual inventory, while an unlicensed individual may not make any entry into or adjust it.

Screens new employees before employment where they may work in or around areas where controlled substances are handled, keeps the documentation available to the Commissioner on request, and does not knowingly employ any agent or employee barred by 105 CMR 700.005(B)(2).

Gives written notice to the Field Division Office of the Administration in its area within one business day of discovery and files a complete and accurate DEA Form 106 within 45 calendar days, reporting whether or not the substances are later recovered.

role_duties.role: Supplier of a shipment lost in transit
role_duties.duty: Reports an in-transit loss by its agent or by the common or contract carrier it selected within one business day of discovery, except where the theft or loss occurs during an import or export transaction.

role_duties.role: The two employees required at a destruction or transfer
role_duties.duty: Load and unload or observe the loading and unloading until a transfer is complete, accompany the substances where the registrant transports them, handle or observe the handling until the substance is rendered non-retrievable, and personally witness the destruction where 21 CFR 1317.95(c) or (d) applies.

Holds its own registration with the Administration, accepts delivery only at its registered location with personal receipt by an employee and no re-routing once en route, stores the substances under the security controls in parts 1301 and 1317, and destroys or causes the destruction of substances received for destruction no later than 30 calendar days after receipt.

role_duties.role: Registrant that destroyed or caused destruction
role_duties.duty: Maintains the DEA Form 41 record of destruction, complete and accurate, with the name and signature of the two witnessing employees.

common_traps.text: Adjusting the perpetual inventory to match a count, which resolves the paperwork and destroys the evidence; 247 CMR 9.21(8) sends a discrepancy to the Manager of Record to investigate and restricts who may make the adjustment at all.
Collapsing the two federal clocks into one, so the written notice waits for the Form 106; the notice is due within one business day of discovery and the Form 106 within 45 calendar days after it.
Treating recovery of the stock, or identification of the person responsible, as something that cancels the report, when the paragraph requires the report whether or not either happens.

Looking for a numerical threshold of significance instead of applying the factors the regulation actually lists, among them quantity in relation to the type of business, association with access by specific individuals, and any pattern of losses over a specific time period.

Reading the theft-or-loss duty in this section as covering anything other than controlled substances; the theft or loss of DEA order forms is a separate duty that belongs with the ordering rules and is not reached here.

Treating a DEA Form 41 as the receipt for anything leaving the pharmacy for disposal, when 21 CFR 1304.21(e) attaches it to destruction under 21 CFR 1317.95(d) and to causing destruction under 21 CFR 1317.95(c) and to nothing else.

Forgetting that the same form appears twice for different reasons, once as the record of a destruction and once as the copy a practitioner submits to the Special Agent in Charge to request disposal assistance.
Assuming a pharmacy may drive unwanted stock to an incinerator itself, when transport by the registrant's own means to a destruction location is written into 21 CFR 1317.05(b) for non-practitioners.
Accepting a disposal vendor on the strength of its business description or a state permit rather than confirming that it is registered with the Administration as a reverse distributor.

Believing that removing labels, crushing tablets or mixing stock into ordinary waste satisfies the destruction standard, when the substance must be rendered non-retrievable by a permanent and irreversible alteration of its physical or chemical condition.

Skipping the second employee, or having one person witness while the other only signs afterwards, when 21 CFR 1317.95 requires two employees at each stage and personal witnessing of the destruction under paragraphs (c) and (d).

Moving expired or quarantined stock out of secured storage because it can no longer be dispensed, when 247 CMR 9.21(10) applies every requirement of the section to substances that are expired, quarantined, or pending reverse distribution.

Reading the screening duty in 105 CMR 700.005(B) as an ordinary background check, when the regulation states that it is made solely to determine whether the prospective employee can be trusted to work in and around controlled substances.
Importing a look-back period into 105 CMR 700.005(B)(2), or trying to answer an absolute bar with restricted duties, a documented history or a notification, none of which the paragraph provides.
